turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: We will hear argument first this morning in Case 25-1083, Mullin versus Doe, and the consolidated case. General Sauer.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Respondents here seek judicial review of the Secretary's decisions to terminate temporary protected status for Syria and Haiti. Yet Section 1254a(b)(5)(A) provides that there is no judicial review of any determination of the Secretary with respect to the designation or termination or extension of a designation of a foreign state for temporary protected status. That provision means what it says. "Determination" is hardly a rarely used word that broadly includes the Secretary's decisions, conclusions, or opinions. Both "any" and "with respect to" have an expansive meaning and a broadening effect. The provision thus bars judicial review of both the Secretary's ultimate decision whether to designate, extend, or terminate and of each antecedent step along the way to that determination. Respondents' attempts to carve out exceptions to the review bar would eviscerate it because virtually any substantive challenge could be recast as a procedural claim, as their own claims demonstrate. Moreover, their claims plainly cannot be raised without referring to or relying on the termination decisions, and they challenge the very kind of foreign-policy-laden judgments that are traditionally entrusted to the political branches. Even if their claims are not barred, they are meritless. The statute does not micromanage the degree of consultation with other agencies. Paragraph (b)(3) requires the Secretary to consider the national interest in reviewing designations made under (b)(1)(C) because it requires her to determine whether the foreign state continues to meet the conditions for designation under paragraph (1). Far from demonstrating pretext, the fact that the Secretary exercised her discretion consistently is a virtue, not a vice. And the Miot Respondents' constitutional claim is meritless under any standard of review. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: What was the practice before the -- this statute was adopted?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: That was the EVD practice --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- that's discussed in the Smith -- the en banc Smith decision from the D.C. Circuit. And that was, I think, properly characterized by Judge Silberman in his opinion as essentially a forbearance policy that fell within the heartland of Heckler against Cheney. So one of the points we make is that the historical background of this statute is a statute where there was limited, if any, judicial review of executive discretion in that case. And it's telling that President Bush, in his signing statement, objected to Congress moving into this area and entrenching on what he viewed as the executive's traditionally unreviewable discretion. So it's unsurprising in that context that Congress passed a judicial review bar that at least partially accommodated the executive's constitutional objection to the sort of imposition of these kinds of regulations in that particular area.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: If the President or the executive branch has constitutional authority to do this in a discretionary way, can Congress limit that?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: We don't dispute that here. President Bush obviously objected on that ground. But we don't dispute that Congress can move in here. And what -- and what they've done, as we envision it, they have moved into an area that was really kind of a forbearance or an enforcement policy regime, and they've elevated it to a particular status and said here are the criteria for regulating that status. And we don't dispute that Congress has the authority to do that.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Are there -- are there any examples of that discretionary authority being challenged?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: You mean in this particular case or more generally?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: More generally.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Well, there is the DED -- I'm not sure if this is responsive to the question, but there is the DED policy that's kind of a -- as I understand it, a -- a successor of the EVD. I won't call it a -- I guess program, you could call it, from -- from the 1908s. So there are situations where the executive exercises enforcement discretion here. When it comes to TPS, Congress has entered the area, has created it as a particular immigration status, and we don't -- we don't dispute that Congress can do that here.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Counsel, do you --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: General, you rely on Trump versus Hawaii in -- in your argument, but that involved the President and entry restrictions. Here, we're concerned with the Secretary and -- and aliens that are already present -- present. Your argument is a significant expansion of Trump versus Hawaii, isn't it?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Well, I point to what the Court said in the particular paragraph where it discusses why rational basis review would apply here as opposed to a more stringent review under Arlington Heights. The Court pointed to features like this is neutral on its face, which we have here; it's within the core of the executive responsibility, which we also have here; it's freighted with foreign relations concerns and national security concerns. Those kinds of criteria are all present here. Obviously, as the Court correctly -- as you point -- correctly point out, the President was involved and it was an exclusion as opposed to people who are already here under a -- under a kind of status. However, the Court did go on to say that -- that Trump versus Hawaii applies across different contexts and constitutional claims. And the cases that it cited, like Kleindienst against Mandel and -- and the other -- Mathews against Diaz and other cases that are cited there are also cases that weren't -- didn't have those particular features of it. So, for those reasons, we think Trump against Hawaii provides the proper, the rational basis standard for their constitutional claim. However, if the Court goes the other way, we also claim that, as I said before, that's meritless under any standard of review.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Can I take you back to the EVD discussion that you had with Justice Thomas? Although President Bush may have objected to the restrictions and the intent to cabin the Secretary's discretion, wasn't it Congress's view that the EVD program was seriously flawed -- in fact, I'm quoting now from the legislative history -- "seriously flawed and in urgent need of reform"?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: That certainly may have been the views of some legislators. What we know is --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: No, I'm talking about the House report, that the reason why the TPS came into being and we still don't have the EVD unregulated scheme was because Congress was concerned about the fact that, for example, "the conditions under which safe haven may be granted, extended, or terminated do not appear in any regulation," that it appeared as though the executive was exercising its discretion in an unregulated fashion, and so Congress created this statute in order to restrict the executive. And wasn't that the reason why President Bush was objecting to it?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Well, I can't speak for President Bush. I don't dispute most of what you said. We do believe Congress moved into an area where there was really, you know, a perception at least of kind of unfettered discretion, unregulation, set forth sort of broad and highly discretionary criteria in which the --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: All right. So are those reviewable in your view? Now we have a statute in which Congress has clearly required the Secretary to take certain statutory steps, to include, for example, consultation. Are those reviewable in your view?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: What is not reviewable is any determination with respect to --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I'm asking you what is reviewable. Is it reviewable for a person to allege that the Secretary made this determination without following the statutory steps?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Certainly not.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Not?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: That would be a determination with respect to a -- for example, here, a -- a -- a termination of --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So what was the point of Congress putting this statute into being and having requirements for the Secretary if there was no ability for anyone to challenge the Secretary's compliance?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Congress may presume, as this Court frequently does, that the executive would -- would be presumed to act within the bounds of -- that it set forth, and Congress provided for ongoing congressional oversight. So there's an annual reporting requirement. There is a 6- to 18-month situation. So, in a sense, judicial review is kind of a misfit with this particular statute because the Secretary has to go back every 18 months and reconsider and reconsider, and judicial review, as we see here --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: What -- what do you do -- what do you do with the precedents of this Court -- and I'm thinking about Bowen and I'm thinking about -- gosh, there was another one -- in which we don't agree that a determination is what you're saying it is? In other words, you know, in Bowen, we specifically indicated that -- and it used very similar language -- and we said, let's see -- Bowen used the language any determination of the amount of benefits under the Medicare statute was in the judicial review bar. And we said that provision "simply does not speak to the" -- "to challenges mounted against the method by which such amounts are to be determined rather than the determinations themselves." We drew a clear distinction that included the word and concept of determination. So how do you distinguish that from this?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: As to Bowen, the statute in Bowen actually had an affirmative grant of the power to judicial review, so as to the Part A Medicare benefits that were at issue there, the stat -- the statute said we are affirmatively granting judicial review of those to an extent. And then, in a prior case, this Court in Erica had said we infer -- we -- we -- we -- we sort of imply from that that there is no judicial review of Part B. Then, when it came to Bowen, the Court said we're not going to take that negative inference and hold that that, you know --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: General, can I --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- satisfied the traditional review.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Your position seems to be, and you said it in your opening, any step in the process is not subject to judicial review. If the Secretary posted a notice on X saying, "I hereby terminate Syria's TPS effect" -- "TPS program effective tomorrow," you would say that there's no judicial review of that decision, right?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That means that even though the statutory requirements required her to post this not on X but on the Federal Register, it requires that TPS holders be given 60 days' notice of the termination, it requires that she consult with department agencies, and she doesn't, let's assume it, all right? That none of those procedural steps required by the statute are reviewable, that's your position?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Correct. And we would -- or I would venture that it's procedural, yeah.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. So the agency could have said the -- Congress could have said any termination of TPS status is unreviewable. But it didn't. It did a different formulation. It did determination of termination. That seems to me very close to McNary, where we said you can't challenge the substantive conclusion, but you can challenge the procedural or policies underlying that choice. I don't see how you differentiate McNary.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I would say -- I would point to three things to distinguish McNary. And keep in mind, our position is that there is no McNary exception here at all, but if there is, the Court disagrees, they don't fit within that.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, but -- but what you're -- what -- what you're basically saying is Congress wrote a statute for no purpose because it set forth procedural steps that had to be followed and the Constitution, as we have said, due process applies to any alien who lives in the United States. It applies to all people living here -- I know you have said unlawfully, but at least these people until the termination are here lawfully and with permission. They're entitled to due process. And now Congress has given them a process. It may not be a court process, but that's okay. It's a process. And you're saying that the President -- it's unreviewable whether the President has followed that process.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: The Secretary. And what Congress says there is --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, I mean --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Counsel, you -- excuse me. You said a moment ago that there were three points in response to the -- my colleague's question. Could you just briefly mention those?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Sure. Yeah. Two buckets and the first has three points. So the first bucket is we say there is no McNary exception that's implied by this statute. And McNary differs in text, there's textual differences in the statute. There's the subject matter, the sort of decision that is exempt here with judicial review as I said at the beginning is the sort of thing that is traditionally, you know, entrusted to the political branches. And then there's the historical background that we -- we -- we -- I discussed with Justice Thomas in the beginning. So, if you look at the textual differences, a determination where both McNary and Reno said that determination is used in a specialized sense --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- in that particular statute is different than any determination with respect to.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you. Got it.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So I'm not quite sure, and not so long ago you came in and said that every executive officer has to be answerable to the President. So the President's statements have to be attributable to its executive officers, to the Secretary. I don't see how you can take both positions.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Either an executive follows the President's orders or it doesn't.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I -- I would point to what the Court said or at least the Chief Justice's opinion in Regents discussed this and said the President's at a certain remove from this decision. The statute places this, invests this decision in the Secretary, and the Secretary is --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But the Secretary here, Noem, said she was following the President's policy. That's what she announced when she was reviewing these items.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I think --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So I don't know how we can't attribute what the President had said his policy is when she herself says she's following it.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: We know what the President directed her to do because it's in the executive order, 14159, the invasion proclamation, where the President said specifically respected TPS that she should ensure that or he now, but she should --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But that doesn't -- but that doesn't give her a right to do what I started with, which is to announce the termination of this policy in contravention of every procedural step, which was the hypothetical I gave you. You're saying that's not reviewable.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: But baked into the very concept of a judicial review bar is the possibility that the -- the decision that's not subject to judicial review might be based -- totally baseless, arbitrary, you know, wrongly decided or -- or -- or really crazy.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, that's true, General --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: General --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: -- but -- but I guess the question is in what? I -- I mean, this judicial review bar is a broad one, means something. If -- if there's a completely arbitrary understanding of what the country conditions are, there's nothing a court can do about that, right? So, you know, basically, Congress has said this can be the weirdest, strangest, most arbitrary conclusion as to country conditions, and the courts still can't do anything. So point taken there. But that's a different thing than to say that all the things that the statute says that the Secretary is supposed to do in order to determine country conditions are themselves unreviewable. I'm sorry, I'm losing my voice. Because what the statute says is, look, she shall review country conditions after consultation, and if she decides I don't feel like consulting and, more to the point, I don't even feel like reviewing country conditions, I want to do some completely different kind of analysis to determine whether to make this designation, is it really feasible that Congress meant for those decisions to be unreviewable?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I think --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I'm really sorry. Go ahead. And, you know, the likelihood of my asking a follow-up is very --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: -- is very diminished.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Congress said any -- any determination with respect to designation, extension, or termination is not subject to judicial review. In EPA against Calumet, this Court talked about --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Right. But the determination -- you see, I'm already going.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I mean, the determination can refer straight back to what the Secretary is supposed to determine, which is whether the conditions for designation continue to be met. Okay. That's it.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I mean, they make an argument like this. They say determination is used in a specialized sense in the statute. I just think that textually is baseless. I mean, by my count, "determination" is used in this -- this one statutory section in five different senses. It talks about things about your eligibility for benefits. That's a determination. Admissibility, that's a determination. Whether there's extreme hardship, that's a determination.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But does that hurt you or help you? I mean, I'll -- I'll pick up where Justice Kagan left off. You know, we -- we have specific things in the statute that Congress says the Secretary has discretion to determine. And then Congress also has parts of the statute that directs the Secretary specifically with respect to the steps that she is to take in order to make those determinations. So I -- I just think you're kind of struggling against what seems to be the most obvious way and the most straightforward way to understand this statute, which is that when the judicial review bar says that the courts cannot review the determinations of the Secretary, it is referencing the things, the substantive conclusions that the Secretary must make under the statute. And some of them are, you know, not the ultimate. Some of them are findings. For example, the Secretary has to make certain findings, says the statute. And I could see how those could be determinations. So it's not that we're just looking for the word "determination" in the statute, but we're understanding that Congress has directed this Secretary in this statute, in contrast with the prior regime, to make certain findings, make certain determinations, and here is how you go about doing it. And so my question is, when someone says the Secretary has not followed those steps, they didn't -- she didn't consult, she didn't put it in the right place in terms of notice -- this is Justice Sotomayor's example -- it's very hard, I think, to say that the judicial review bar, which speaks only to the determinations of the Secretary, precludes that kind of claim.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Two points. "Determination" is a broad term, as the Court held in EPA against Calumet, that encompasses any decision, opinion, or conclusion. So --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Including the decision not to follow the steps? That's your point?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Right. When it says any -- I'd say two things about that. When it says "any determination with respect to," here, a termination decision --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: It means any --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- the --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- decision not to follow the steps that we've put in the statute?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: So, if there is a determination that, oh, I don't think there are any appropriate agencies to consult with here and, therefore, I'm not to consult, that's a determination within the plain meaning of that term. But, more fundamentally, it -- it bars judicial review -- certainly, everyone concedes it bars judicial review of that final determination. And look at it in the context of this case, where both sets of plaintiffs have filed complaints saying --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Yes, we can see that, but that's -- they're saying that's not all the kinds of claims we'd like to make. And we're just now focusing on the kinds of claims that aren't the final determination. There, the Secretary's decision -- and I had a hypothetical -- to pull out a Ouija board. The Secretary says, you know how I'm going to figure this out? I'm going to -- another example -- put Syria in a hat and, you know, Haiti in a hat on a slip of paper and all the countries, and I'll pull out the ones that get TPS and I -- that's not following the statutory steps. She's made a determination to do that. And your view would be that no judicial review of that -- of that claim?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: And any exception that the Court would craft here would be something that a truck could be driven through. And that's what we see in the lower courts, and that's what we see in the briefing in this case.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: All right. Okay.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I mean, look, for example, at --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: General, can I ask you a question? You seem to concede that the constitutional claims are not barred by this very same provision. Is that right? And, if so, why?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: We are -- under Webster against Doe, Demore against Kim, and so forth, we have disputed that there be -- may be a little extra clear statement that would be required to exclude constitutional claims. We just haven't disputed that in this case. We're not asking the Court to revisit Webster, for example, in this case.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: So you think Webster is on all fours with this?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I don't know if it's on all fours. We think Webster and Demore are strong enough to indicate that under those cases, we'd have to be fighting with those cases, so to speak, to argue that there's no judicial review of the constitutional claims here. And, here, of course, we think the constitutional claims -- it's not -- not a close call, basically. But we have not disputed that. We -- we -- we don't argue that the judicial review bar extends to the constitutional claim.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So, counsel, let's go back to the Chief's question on Hawaii. Assume that I disagree with you and that Arlington Heights applies because Hawaii and all of the cases that you cited supporting it involve aliens coming into the United States, not aliens in the United States. So let's assume that I believe that due process requires some process for aliens who are here to be removed. Then we can argue about what that process is and -- and how binding it is or not. But, if it's Arlington Heights, a discriminatory purpose just needs to be a reason, not the only reason for acting, correct?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: A motivating factor, I think, is what it says.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Motivating factor. Now this Court has explained an additional purpose to discriminate against poor whites would not render nugatory the purpose to discriminate against all blacks. Now we have a President saying at one point that Haiti is a "filthy, dirty, and disgusting S-hole country." I'm quoting him. And where he complained that the United States takes people from such countries instead of people from Norway, Sweden, or Denmark, where he declared illegal -- where he declared illegal immigrants, which he associated with TPS, as poisoning the blood of America. I don't see how that one statement is not a prime example of the Arlington example at work and showing that a discriminatory purpose may have played a part in this decision.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: All the statements that they cite as to the Secretary and as to the President -- obviously, there's an issue there about which one you're going to weigh more heavily -- none of them, not a single one of them, mentions race or relates to race in any way.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, it -- it certainly does when you're saying we're taking the -- we're taking people from these countries' TPS program, which are all non-white, but, instead, we should be taking people from Norway, Sweden, or Denmark. It -- it seems to me that that's as close to the Arlington example as you can get.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: All those statements in context refer to problems like crime, poverty, welfare dependence, drugs, drug importation.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, but the -- the Arlington example is yes, I don't want poor people, but not all people from Norway, Sweden, or Denmark are necessarily rich, but they are all virtually white.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: The Chief Justice's opinion in Regents, for example, refers to actually some of the very same statements that they allege here, statements that are now nine, 10 years sold.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: But Regents -- Regents applied a very different standard of review because of the nature of the applicant. This is a very different question. This is whether a race-based classification could -- can be or should be permitted to be a motivating factor.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I strongly disagree with that. Regents assumed that Arlington Heights would apply, and it said these kinds of statements are unilluminating. They, you know, raise no plausible inference of discriminatory animus. Yeah?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: General, what about poisoning the blood of Americans?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: If you -- if you look at those statements in context, again, they're clearly talking about problems like crime --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: What about bad genes, "bad genes"?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Again, poverty --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Also not -- not racially --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Yes. Yeah, they -- they -- they presented them wrenched from context. You can look at each one of those statements. They're talking about problems of crime, poverty, welfare dependency, again, problems that have been emphasized again and again by not just President Trump, not just the Secretary, but many others who favor a tough immigration policy. And if the position of the district courts here --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So your -- the position of the United States is that we have to have an actual racial epithet, that we don't -- we aren't allowed to look at all the contexts, to include the President's insistence that immigrants from certain countries, largely, if not almost exclusively, countries with African immigrants, black African immigrants, are not allowed, and -- and calling these sorts of names and the types of things he said about Haiti, at the same time that it is the policy of the United States to encourage and welcome immigrants from places like Norway and Denmark and white South -- South Africans, your view is that it's not appropriate for the Court to take into account that kind of evidence or the context in which all of this is happening?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: It's our view that those statements that they allege, which include statements that were before the Court in both Trump against Hawaii and Regents -- keep in mind this is the third time this kind of claim has come before this Court. It rejected it in Trump against Hawaii, rejected it again in Regents --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Right. But the immigration policy, the idea -- the white South African immigration policy is recent. So that wasn't in Trump against Hawaii. That wasn't -- the statements about Haiti and eating pets and the names that were called with respect to these immigrants even though they are lawfully in the United States, that -- those are pretty recent. So let's separate it out then. What do you say about those kinds of things?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Again, by the -- as the Court held in Regents, these are statements made in different contexts that are remote in time. They are unilluminating. The Court said in Regents, the Chief Justice's opinion in Regents says we're going to give them the most negative possible interpretation. That's provided by the --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I'm giving it the most negative interpretation. So tell me my -- if I assume or think that these are related to the President's intentions to encourage certain immigrants on the basis of race and discourage others, what do we do with that in light of Arlington Heights?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: The Court should conclude that the statements are unilluminating and fail to raise any plausible inference of animus.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: That's not what Judge -- Judge Reyes found that they were illuminating. Aren't we applying a clear error standard here? What do we do -- we're not looking at this de novo. We have a district court finding that there is evidence of discriminatory intent here, enough early in the case to allow this claim to go forward. So aren't we bound in some regard with respect to what the lower court has already determined about these facts?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I would say --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: No?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- I don't -- I don't concede that, but it does not matter.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: You think there's not --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Under any standard of review --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: It's not clear error review?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- the Court's looking at exactly the same statements that -- that -- that she is looking at. The Court should apply the logic of Regents, which says, first of all, the President's statements are less relevant; the Secretary's statements are what matter. Again, these kinds of statements don't refer to race.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So ignore the findings of fact of the lower court, do not give them any deference, no clear error review, we're just looking at this afresh?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I think it does not -- it does not matter with deference or without deference. This claim just doesn't get off the starting blocks. It's the third time this sort of claim has been brought. The lower courts are enamored of these kinds of claims, but this is the third time this kind of claim has come before this Court. It's rejected it in Hawaii, rejected it in Regents, should be rejected again here. It's not --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: General, can I --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So, General, maybe -- maybe --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: -- ask you a question about -- oh.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I'm sorry, go ahead.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: No, no, no.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: No, no, no, go ahead, I'll have more time to recover.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I wanted to take you to the procedural objection. Let's say that you lose on your argument that even the process that the Secretary followed to terminate is not subject to judicial review. What would -- take your best crack at articulating what standards a court would apply when reviewing the sufficiency of the consultation.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: In other words, if -- if the argument is that the consulting claim alone is procedural and reviewable?

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Is reviewable, is -- yeah, yeah, yeah. So we have this exchange, the email exchange, in Miot. I mean, what -- what -- take your best crack at --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I think --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: -- articulating the standards by which a court would review that.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Again, I think this Court should go to the dictionary definition of "consult." And you see this actually in the Syria brief, where they concede that seeking input is consultation. Seeking advice from someone knowledgeable is a form of consultation. And keep in mind it's not just consult. It also says appropriate. So the word "appropriate," the Court's held in other contexts, confers broad discretion. So the Secretary could decide, I don't think there are any appropriate agencies to talk to here. You know, again, that would be within -- assuming reviewability, which we strongly disagree with --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Right. Okay. Taken.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- but even there, again, it's -- it's a weak claim. It's -- this -- the phrase after -- it says three times after consultation with appropriate agencies the Secretary is going to do a bunch of things. And what you have here is the district courts. They initially said she didn't consult at all. But it turns out that she did. There is an exchange with the Department of State. So now they're saying, well, that wasn't quite enough, it wasn't meaningful enough. You see how substance has already crept back into even this case, not --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: What -- what would happen -- what would happen, General, if the original email had been sent out and no response came back? Would that also be appropriate consultation?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Absolutely, yes. In other words, she can't force the Secretary of or -- or -- or the State Department to respond and so, for that reason, yes, that would be appropriate consultation too.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Suppose it were the response that came back said, I've got to run some traps here in the building, we'll get you an answer by Wednesday, and then the Secretary made her determination on Tuesday.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Consultation has happened on her end. And, again, she cannot force the state to provide -- State Department to provide a timely response. The -- the statute regulates what the Secretary does, not what Department of State does.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Even though the Secretary was, like, well on her way to getting a timely response?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: And, again, if you've asked, you -- you've consulted. And, here, of course, we have an exchange where there's a prompt response.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Suppose that, you know, the -- the -- the question is made -- the question is proffered, and then the -- the response comes back, wasn't that baseball game tonight great, last night great?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Again, State can say something completely unresponsive. If she sought input from State, she has consulted. And, again, this is the sort of discretionary call that for very good reasons the statute vests in the Secretary. How much do I need to talk, which agencies do I talk to, is this response good enough? Again, in this case, in the South Sudan example, she said, you know what, I want some more information, I haven't heard back. She did the exact -- I mean, that's really the hypothetical.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: And then -- and then your -- your -- I think you said that even if the Secretary didn't ask the question, she could have just decided not to ask the question and that would be appropriate consultation too?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: If she doesn't ask at all, I don't think I would say that that's consultation.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I thought you said --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I would say that's not subject to judicial review. But she --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I thought -- I -- assuming it's subject to judicial review. I -- I -- I had thought that you said that she could have decided that there was no person whose opinions mattered.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Yeah. No, if there's a determination that none of the agencies is appropriate, then as opposed to there is an appropriate agency, but I decline to consult with them, that would be the distinction that I would raise.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Okay. But, as to everybody else, as long as you ask a question, whether or not you wait for the answer, whether or not you give them appropriate time for the answer, whatever the answer is, whether the answer is on a completely unrelated topic, it just doesn't matter?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: That would fall within the plain meaning of the word "consultation, as we argue, and, again --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I mean, really? The plain meaning of the word "consultation"? Like, the plain meaning of the word "consultation" seems to me like you consult with somebody on a topic. That means you ask a question. They give an answer that's on the same topic. You know, it doesn't have to be long. You don't have to lock a person in the room together for three hours. But, I mean, you have to ask the question: Hey, what are country conditions like? And then the answer comes back country conditions are fine or they're not fine. You know, that's appropriate consultation. I'm not, like, asking for the moon, but, you know, what are country conditions like? Weren't the Dodgers great last night? That does not seem like appropriate consultation.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: To seek advice or input is consultation. And with -- with respect to the example of locking them in the room for three hours, that's kind of the road that the district courts are going down. They're saying you did check with it, but it wasn't meaningful enough, so we give you kind of a D-plus on your consultation.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, but that's not the road I'm going down. I mean, I guess I said that because that's not the road I'm going down. And, you know, sometimes consultation is very thorough and sometimes in government it's not very thorough. But, if Congress says to consult about a particular subject matter, then it seems as though what Congress said was you should ask somebody and they should give an answer.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Certainly, you should ask somebody. The statute doesn't say she can compel them to give an answer and she did ask. So regardless of what --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But, General, the statute does go a little further than that. I mean, you keep homing in on the word "consultation." But, if we read what the statute says, and I'm paraphrasing the relevant part, "after consultation with appropriate agencies of the government, the Secretary shall review the conditions in the foreign state for which a designation is in effect and such" -- "and shall determine whether the conditions for such designation continue to be met." So, surely, the consultation, however long or short, can't be about something other than country conditions. I mean, if you read the whole sentence, what she's consulting about is her determination as to whether the country conditions are still in effect.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I think what she's consulting about is a little more specific than that. She -- it says, you know, after consultation with appropriate agencies, she shall assess the country conditions and determine whether or not the criteria set forth in subsection 1 are still met. So the consultation can relate to not just country conditions but anything else that is relevant to that.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But you just said with Justice Kagan it can relate to baseball. What I'm trying to do is figure out whether this statute, when it requires consultation, at least requires some exchange of information concerning this subject, whether the country conditions are still met.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I believe I said, if the response has to do with baseball, there's really nothing she can do about that. She still consulted. If she sends an email to State and says, hey, what do you think of the Dodgers, I don't think we would argue that that constitutes consultation, because I think you correctly pointed out the context of that statute. Now it's not just country conditions. It's the entire determination whether or not the -- the -- the criteria for designation under subsection 1 are still met. If she's seeking input about that, she has consulted. I see my time's up.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, General. Justice Thomas, anything further? Justice Alito? Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: General, I don't think you -- I know -- General --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I'm sorry.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Party's over. No, you've got to stay there.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I'm very sorry.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. You're not disputing that the email exchange of July 21st and July 22nd with respect to Syria and September 5th with respect to Hawaii, where the Secretary asked the State Department to discuss country conditions, that that was the extent of the consultation, correct?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I believe that's what's in the administrative record for both cases. Obviously, one case comes to the Court where the administrative record was -- appears later. There's two different email exchanges. The one in the Syria case says we're re-reviewing country conditions with respect to this country. The other one I believe is in the Haiti case says we're, you know, considering -- or I don't remember the exact words, but considering the following four countries.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Right. But the point is that that was the extent of it? There was no other information that the State Department provided?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: We haven't pointed to anything else in the administrative record to satisfy that consultation requirement.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: All right. And so the question is, if we believe the statute by its terms requires specific consultation with respect to country conditions as opposed to foreign policy concerns, there was no information addressed by the Department of State with respect to the country conditions?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I disagree because, obviously, sending aliens back based on country conditions raises all kinds of foreign policy issues. So, if you say no foreign policy concerns, then --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That -- that's -- well, no, because you're also taking the position that irrespective or regardless of -- I think I just made up -- I used a grammatically incorrect word -- regardless of whether country conditions were bad or not, our national interests required termination, correct?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Yes.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So we can't assume that the State Department that doesn't answer the question presented is actually describing country conditions?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Yeah. And I think I would stand on what I said in response to Justice Jackson, which is that the consultation relates to not just the assessment of country conditions but the entire determination, as that very same sentence goes on to say, to whether or not the conditions under subsection 1 are met.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The only thing -- I'm looking at Haiti. The only thing asked for, we are reviewing country conditions in Haiti. Can you advise on State's views on that matter? I mean, all right. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch, anything further? Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Can you explain the reasons why Congress would have barred judicial review as broadly as you assert?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: I -- I'd emphasize two. There are several. I think perhaps most importantly, the kind of determination that is at issue here is just the sort of determination that lies kind of at the heartland of what has been traditionally entrusted to the political branches. And given -- let me give you a couple examples of that. If you consider, for example, the determination that is made in both of the termination orders that these are nations that have emerged from difficult times and there are new fledgling governments there. And, for example, in the Syria determination, the Secretary says it's our foreign policy to project a message of confidence to the fledgling government of Syria. The president has taken away sanctions. He has recognized that government. There's refugees returning from all over the world. And if we don't terminate TPS, it will send a message of doubt about that country. That that's the sort of foreign-policy-freighted decision that lies at the heartland of the political branch's competence. And it's the sort of thing that you -- as you see in this case, those sorts of determinations being second-guessed by the district courts, it's almost like these district courts are appointing themselves junior varsity Secretaries of State saying I -- I second-guess that. So, if you look at the whole package here --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Well, that's Syria and the Assad regime. I understand that one.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Do you want to give a similar answer on Haiti?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Very similar answer, very similar points are made as to Haiti. I'd emphasize to the Court, if you look at Footnote 35 in the Haiti termination and the accompanying text where it talks about the problem of ongoing chain migration out of Haiti, there's an ongoing exodus, and they argue in this case that the TPS holders are some of the most educated, some of the most law-abiding, some of the sort of best and the brightest that are in diaspora. That Footnote 35 cites an article that she relied on, "Engaging the Haitian Diaspora," where it talks about how, in neighboring Caribbean countries, the United States, and Canada, there are hundreds of thousands of Haitian nationals who are abroad -- you know, who are abroad now. And the determination, this notion that there's ongoing chain migration, the concern is are we actually creating, contributing to the problem, creating a self-fulfilling prophecy by ensuring that there's an indefinite expectation of all those people. There's this kind of talent drain out of Haiti. That's the sort of, like, foreign policy freighted -- that is weighing incommensurables under conditions of uncertainty, that is the sort of foreign-policy-freighted decision and determination that's naturally left to the political branches. So there can be hypotheticals about, you know, the Secretary could do something lawless or crazy, and Congress has a way, has tools to address that because there's annual reports. In the annual report, she's not going to say or he's not going to say I flipped a coin. The annual report's going to have to give reasons. And if Congress --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: The annual reports would be after the fact, so --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: That is true, but --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: -- the concern you've heard here is that's already done then.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: It is done, but it has to be reviewed every 18 months. And that structure itself kind of makes judicial review a misfit because judicial review takes more than 18 months. So, if we're put under a preliminary injunction, as we saw in the Ramos litigation, you know, from 2018 through 2020, even though there's supposed to be this ongoing 18-month re-review, the district -- the district courts enter -- they put in an injunction, and all of a sudden you have this sort of extended thing. Keep in mind this is temporary protected status. The word "temporary" is used again and again in the statute, including its title. And we're looking at a situation where there have been initial designations that go back to 1991 in the case of Somalia, Hurricane Mitch in 1998, 20 -- 27 years ago, as to Honduras and Nicaragua, and these were still in effect until -- still are in effect. So there's a sense that -- and one very important point I'd make there is, if you look at Haiti specifically, the Haitian termination has now been enjoined twice, both in the first Trump administration and in this administration. And so the judicial review is having this effect of really defeating the fundamental purpose of the statute, which is inherently temporary. There's this very frequent periodic review.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So I have no doubt that there are foreign policy considerations, but do you dispute that the thrust of this statute is actually the humanitarian concern, that the initial designation under this statute is supposed to be a consideration of whether there is an ongoing armed conflict within the state, and due to such a conflict, returning the aliens who are nationals of that state would pose a "serious threat" to their personal safety? It seems to me that this statute does allow the Secretary to take into the account -- into account the kinds of things that you discussed with Justice Kavanaugh but against the backdrop of the actual purpose of the statute, which is what conditions are in this country and whether or not it would be safe to return those people. And so I -- I guess I'm just struggling with your argument that the Secretary can make this determination without, as a procedural matter, taking into account country conditions as the statute requires.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: The Secretary is obligated to consider country conditions under (b) -- of various kinds, different kinds of country conditions under (b)(1)(A), (b)(1)(B), and (b)(1)(C).

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And if she doesn't, you say not reviewable?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Not reviewable. Under (b)(1)(C), most relevant, she considers not just country conditions but also whether allowing the aliens to stay here would be contrary to the United States' national interests. If anything is discretionary, if anything exudes deference --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Yes, you're picking that part of the statute --

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- to the Secretary, that language does.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- but I've read -- I've read other parts of the statute that require her to do country conditions. And you're saying, if she doesn't, that's not reviewable; see the other parts of the statute that talk about foreign policy. I just don't understand the concept of the Secretary being constrained to do certain things and not being required to do them in the sense that they're not enforceable. She can basically do whatever she -- she wants, I hear from your argument.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Congress assumed that risk when it said there is no judicial review of any determination --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: All right.

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: -- with respect to termination.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Arulanantham.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: Congress struck a balance in the TPS statute. It granted the Secretary substantial discretion to designate countries at the outset but constrained the authority to terminate TPS once people have come to rely on it through mandatory procedures and rules. Congress struck a corresponding balance on judicial review. It didn't broadly bar review of all policies and procedures or all questions of law and fact, as in neighboring immigration statutes. It barred review of any determination in subsection (b), which are the country conditions assessments on which the Secretary would be expected to have expertise. Congress thus preserved review to ensure compliance with other requirements in the statute, including in subsection (b), like the obligation to consult and to make decisions based on country conditions. The bottom line is this: The Secretary can terminate TPS, but he must turn square corners, follow the rules Congress set. In contrast, as we've heard today, the government reads this statute like a blank check. Today, they want to use it to expel non-citizens, but the power that they seek is a double-edged sword. The Secretary could designate every country from which an undocumented person has come to the United States explicitly to provide mass immigration relief under this statute, and on their view, the courts could do nothing. That contravenes the text, bedrock administrative law, and common sense. On the merits, this is an easy case. One basis for Syria's designation is armed conflict. But the Secretary never consulted the State Department about the armed conflict. Even today, the State Department's website says armed conflict in Syria remains active. In addition, the other basis for Syria's designation, which is extraordinary and temporary conditions, she terminated based on the national interest. But the plain text makes clear that the termination must be based solely on the conditions in the foreign state. Finally, it matters that this case is here on a preliminary relief order that just preserved TPS while the case proceeds. People like Dr. Sara Doe, a pediatrician giving lifesaving care to children, have no later recourse if they are illegally stripped of their work authorization, let alone face detention or deportation. Laila Doe's daughter came here at the age of three and is now about to graduate high school. She should keep her status while the case proceeds. I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Would you be kind enough to say what else is reviewable under -- despite the -- the jurisdiction-stripping provision? Because it seems pretty broad. It says there's no judicial review of any determination of the Attorney General.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So we agree it's broad, Your Honor.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: It bars everything that the Secretary determines in subsection (b). And if you look for the word "determines" in subsection (b), it appears in many places. But there are other words also, like in (b)(3)(A), the Secretary has an obligation after consultation with appropriate agencies. And that is not described as a determination. So we think there's review over consultation. The Secretary also has an -- an obligation to review conditions in the foreign state. So we think that there then should be review over just whether the fact, did she, in fact, review the conditions in the foreign state? Not if she got it right, but did she review it? There are other things in there too. The opening line is "at least 60 days before the end of initial period of designation." So there's a timing rule. When do you get to do this? And, you know, as some of these hypotheticals have suggested, you can't do it immediately. You can't do it -- and so there's review over the timing as well. But -- but it's very minimal. It's only the procedural rules. But I would argue, Your Honor, that in a context where there's no review on the substantive determination, the procedural rules are all the more important then to ensure that we have appropriate government decision-making.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: So, in the case of appellate courts, for example, they have authority to review judgments. Would you, using the same logic, say they can only review the substantive underlying judgment but not the underlying determinations?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No, Your Honor. I -- if I understand the hypothetical correctly, I think it actually favors us because this statute uses the word "determination" as a distinct act from the ultimate order to either extend, designate, or terminate TPS. This is very clear from the termination provision, which is (b)(3)(B). It's the next one after the one which has the consultation rule in it. It says -- and I'll apologize in advance because the words are very -- sound very similar -- it says, if the Attorney General determines -- determines -- that a foreign state no longer meets the conditions for designation, he shall terminate the designation by publishing notice of the determination in the Federal Register. So it's clearly using them as two distinct ideas. One is the determination, that's the country conditions assessment, then the termination order or the extension order or the designation order. They're distinct acts in this context.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Normally, though, we would think that the subsidiary considerations that lead to a judgment would also be reviewable or non-reviewable depending on jurisdiction.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I don't think there's any such general principle of administrative law, Your Honor. We cite the Zuch case just recently in the tax context which literally holds the opposite. It says, you know, the -- the things that make up the determination, the inputs, are different from the output. McNary and Reno v. Catholic Social Services both construed the word "determination" in an immigration statute, contemporaneously with all of this, to distinguish between the determination and the antecedent procedural questions and decision-making criteria, and they relied on Bowen, which we -- we heard discussion of earlier. And I think the last point I'd like to make just on this subject, Your Honor, is even if you might have voted the other way in those cases in the first instance, right, the word "determination" has become embedded in our immigration law with a narrower meaning than what the government ascribes to it here. And you can see that most clearly from the way Congress wrote provisions in 1996, just three years after Catholic Social Services, which is, in turn, two years after McNary. They wrote provisions saying, for example, the expedited removal provisions, they bar review of any individual determination or any other cause or claim related to expedited removal. There's another provision which bars procedures and policies related to expedited removal, in addition to what is already the bar on determination. And then, of course, subsection (b)(9) in the same statute, which Justice Alito's plurality construed in Jennings v. Rodriguez, which we all remember, all questions of law and fact. That's what it bars review of, all questions of law and fact, including substantial statutory and constitutional claims. This is about district court review of removal orders. So they clearly have broader language that they use when they want to cover more than -- when they want to cover all of the antecedent steps.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: And, counsel --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: In order for you to win this case, is it necessary for us to find that the word "determination" in (b)(5)(A) is a term of art?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No, I don't think it's a term of art, Your Honor. I -- I resist that characterization. I do think there's two way -- paths for us to victory.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, let me put it a different way. Would it be necessary for us to say that we give that term in that provision something other than its ordinary meaning in regular speech?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No, Your Honor, I mean, although I do think context is everything, right, when we're construing statutes, and "determination" there we think has to be understood by reference to "determine," which is used eight times in the same subsection to mean country conditions assessment.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Well, I take that to be a yes. We have to -- we have to say, look, "determination" is a very broad word, it's used all the time by -- in -- in many different statutory provisions, it's used all the time by this Court. If we apply ordinary meaning of that term here, I -- I -- I -- I -- I really don't understand how you can prevail.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Well, I guess because I don't think that it always has the full potential breadth that the government has ascribed to it. For example, in this statute, we see it's used two times outside of subsection (b), more than two times but in two sentences outside of subsection (b). And I concede and this was discussed that those are not about country conditions assessments. So it has a different meaning there. But the bar only applies to determinations in subsection (b). And so, again, I think it just means -- it refers back. But my fall-back position, Your Honor, even if you're not willing to say determination should be tied tightly to determine, the two claims in particular, the consultation claim and then the claim about national interest and whether it's appropriately considered at the termination phase, those are the kinds of claims that this Court has considered in administrative law cases going back a hundred years. You know, if you look at the administrative law scholars, the Cox, Rick Hills, and Emma Kaufman brief, it talks about this history. Claims that process is reviewable, even if the ultimate decision is final, have been reviewable in immigration statutes going back to Nishimura Ekiu in 1892. Claims that you've read the wrong criteria into the statute, not whether you got it right, but just are you considering a factor which actually is not the one that's supposed to be considered, those go back to 1904, Gonzales v. Williams and other cases like that. So you could say we're not necessarily giving you that determination that has to be hitched directly to determine, but say we are reading the statute to not be the broadest conceivable jurisdictional bar ever, particularly given that Congress wrote broader ones just a couple of years after this Court had decided McNary and CSS. And that would be at least the first two claims. The consultation claim and the claim about the statutory criteria would be -- which is a pure question of law. I mean, it's just about how you read the statute and how you read the words, is national interest, you know, incorporated into (b)(3) or only in (b)(1). Those claims could be reviewable even under a much narrower theory than our front-line theory, which is that you should use the text and refer to the term --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Counsel, can I give you a hypothetical? Let's imagine that there is a more robust record of consultation here, and the Secretary consults the State Department and the State Department says the country conditions in Syria remain terrible, armed conflict continues, and, you know, I -- I think it would be fine and in the national interest to continue TPS status for Syrian refugees. The Secretary says, yeah, you know what, I'm going to terminate it anyway. Is that reviewable?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So just two thing -- a quick point about your hypo. National interest is not a factor on armed conflict. I just want to flag that for later when we get there.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Okay. Okay. I mean, my point here doesn't really matter.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, entirely.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: I mean, I'm just saying, like, let's imagine that consultation happens, it's a robust consultation, but everything that she hears cuts in favor of keeping TPS status, and she says, I'm terminating it.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: We --

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Is that -- is that reviewable?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: We could not challenge on the ground that she is wrong and the State Department is right. What the statute does is it tries to get the government to speak in one voice, which this Court has said is very important and is a huge problem here when, you know, you have them going back and forth, but if ultimately the Secretary says, you know, speaking in one voice is important, but my people, country conditions people think that the armed conflict is over, so that's what we're doing, that is not reviewable. But what is reviewable is whether she actually asks anything and gets any information about country conditions.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Is this going to get you very much? I mean, if it's just kind of a box-checking exercise, I mean, why would Congress permit review of the procedural aspect when, really, what everybody cares about much more is the substance?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I think it's because Congress and us too and the millions of people who live with TPS holders have some faith in government, and they believe that if there is consultation, the decisions will be better.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: And that's really not unusual, right? I mean, isn't that the whole thrust of something like the APA?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Absolutely.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: That Congress has always sort of understood that agencies are going to have a lot of discretion at the end of the day to make the determinations, but we still need to police to some extent the inputs, what they're looking at, whether they give the public notice and comment, all of the things about procedural rules and requirements for decision-making are important even if the ultimate decision is still left to the agency.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Absolutely, Your Honor. You know, our view is that even if it comes back like a box-checking exercise, people will at least know that somebody talked to somebody else. And it makes sense, of course, DHS has foreign policy expertise. They have their asylum and refugee office and all those people. But the State Department also has a lot of foreign policy expertise and information.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Can I ask --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Would you, I mean, would you, and just to follow up on what Justice Jackson is asking, do you think we can read (b)(5)(A) at least to say we're ruling out APA review here?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Your Honor, I don't want to belabor that point because our brief addresses it at great length. In our view, there is a difference from the Department of Commerce case between whether the record evidence supports the conclusion and whether the decision is motivated by some impermissible criteria. And in Department of Commerce, obviously, the record evidence did support the conclusion, but nonetheless, the decision was based on, you know, a contrived reason. That is the reason why we think pretext claims are reviewable. But it doesn't matter because the first two claims are -- are much more canonically sort of old -- you know, older than SEC v. Chenery. You know, I think that decision really becomes reviewable. This becomes canonical APA law that pretext claims should be understood differently after Chenery I, but these other ideas are much, much older than that, and that's really, you know, all we have to say about it.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, in Department of Commerce, of course, we said that political considerations are a permissible factor. How are we supposed to determine how much political influence is too much?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yeah. I -- I think, in this case, the Secretary said on CNN the day after her first TPS decision that we are taking direction from the direction of the President. He is pausing this program. And after that -- meaning the TPS program. And then there have been 13 terminations in a row. So the district court just said on -- we're here on preliminary relief. I think it's a factual finding for clear error review. The -- the district court said, you know, I think that I will take that statement, when coupled with the confirmatory action of all the TPS terminations and the absence of consultation and all the rest of it, to mean that --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Well, that's a particular circumstance, but, I mean, in general, how would you articulate the principle that this is too much? How do you judge, as a general matter, how much political influence is too much?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Only --

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Not -- not that you're saying, well, it was too much in this case but more generally.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yeah. I mean, I don't think -- I wouldn't change a word of Commerce, Your Honor.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: I wouldn't either.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes. I figured you would say that. And -- and I just -- I just think this is also a very rare outlier case where the Secretary actually said on national television the day after the decision that she was motivated by an impermissible factor. You know, I want to come back to this consultation question, though, to talk about this email. As Justice Sotomayor had said, the entire consultation in this case is reprinted on less than one page, page 41 of our brief.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, could I ask about that particularly? Suppose that there was the same question asked from DHS to State Department, and instead of the answer being State has no foreign policy concerns with ending these TPS designations, suppose the answer was just State has no concerns with ending these TPS designations. Would that be appropriate? Would that be -- would that cross the line into that's fine?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I mean, that is a much harder case than ours because it might be true that no concerns encompasses country conditions, you know, and I'm not saying that definitely that person should win because I think, you know, you -- the -- the government -- I mean the plaintiffs may be entitled to -- to -- to argue that that's not actually what happened there. But our case is so much easier than that because --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Well, is it so much easier? I mean, I wonder -- I mean, the State Department probably says no foreign policy concerns five times before breakfast every day. It's just -- it's -- that's what -- the State Department. They deal with foreign policy concerns. So, if somebody asks them something, they say no foreign policy concerns. Does that really -- is that really going to make the difference between what is permissible consultation and what is not permissible consultation, the fact that they put the words "foreign policy" in the answer?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So -- so two things. First, this same exact worded email, no foreign policy concerns or sometimes they said foreign policy objections, but foreign policy concerns or objections is now the record in seven consecutive TPS terminations under this statute. And that's why all these district courts that they're talking about, right, it's the same thing. So it's not obvious to me that, oh, they could have just written country conditions and they chose to write foreign policy. You know, but, you know, I'd still say turn the square corner and make them -- make them do it. But, beyond that, there is -- you know, we -- we have also --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: When you say that, when you say, look, this is -- this is obviously deliberate language because it was used in seven, what are you suggesting about why they used this language?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So, look, I -- I don't -- I don't know, but I think it is possible that they don't have a foreign policy concern, but they're not comfortable saying that the armed conflict in Syria is over when their own website is saying, if you go to Syria, leave a DNA sample, execute a will before you go, it's active armed conflict, no part of Syria is safe, every part is wracked with violence --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Well, it's not the Assad regime anymore, though. I mean, that -- the whole thing was the Assad regime after 53 years of complete oppression and brutal treatment is gone.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So, Your Honor --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: So do you agree the Assad regime change is a significant change in the history of that country and the -- and the Middle East more broadly?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I mean, of course, anybody would agree with that, Your Honor, but I -- but --

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Okay. Well, that's an important marker then because that's -- that's a big shift in both Syria but also the posture of other countries towards Syria, at least as I -- I don't pretend to be an expert, but that's my understanding of what's the backdrop here.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So -- so two thoughts, Your Honor. Then I want to briefly talk about national interest if -- if there's time. So, first, you know, we're not -- we're not interested in a debate about whether Syria is or is not safe, so, you know, we haven't gotten into that precisely because it's barred by the judicial review bar, right? Our view is they have to consult and that's the end of it. And the second thing I would say is the State Department's own reports believe, of course, Assad -- they recognize Assad has ended, but they say active violence in every part of the country, the daycare that Laila Doe's daughter went to got bombed, the building next to it has been bombed again in southern Syria. That's not the same conflict. It's the Israeli incursion. There's a war between Turkey and Kurdistan -- Kurds going on in the north. There's still lots of conflict according to the State Department's accounts and the -- the CRS report about this. These are in the Joint Appendix. So I don't think it's as simple as that, but we don't contest, if the Secretary says I disagree, Syria is safe, that's fine, but she still has to turn the square corners and follow the steps.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Justice Thomas, anything further?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Just briefly. With respect to the jurisdiction-stripping provision again, if the Secretary actually designates -- does not terminate but designates in favor of -- of a particular group, can others use the exact same objection that you're offering?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I'm not sure I understand the question, Your Honor.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Well, would they be able to challenge the same way that you're challenging --

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I got it.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: -- a positive designation?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Got it. So, no, Your Honor, but not because of the review bar. What they can challenge -- the statute says the Secretary may designate -- this is -- now we're talking about (b)(1), right?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yeah, yeah.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: May designate only if, and then one of these three criteria have to be met.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So, even if a country is horribly in crisis, there's no obligation to designate. And that's the reason why that's unreviewable, you know. But, of course, it doesn't cut the other way, right? On their view, if the Secretary -- this was my opening hypothetical -- if the Secretary designated Mexico for immigration relief, it's unreviewable. On our view, it is reviewable because you look to the -- to the criteria to see whether they actually applied. Did they care at all about conditions, or were they just trying to achieve some political end?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Yeah.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Alito?

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: One of the points that General Sauer made was that if we accept your arguments, it will create a hole in the judicial review bar that you could drive a convoy of trucks through. And you have now said repeatedly that it's necessary for the Secretary to turn square corners, which seems to open -- which seems to support what he says, that if we depart from the ordinary meaning of the review bar, then it is always going to be possible to pick procedural faults in -- to raise procedural objections to what's been done. And what you've said about consultation makes me think that that may be true because, here, there was some consultation. All right, it was very brief and maybe it's not what one would hope for, but still, once you say, well, it's -- it's permissible to review the adequacy of the -- of the consultation, it's always going to be possible to pick -- to -- to raise objections about the adequacy of the -- of the consultation and the words that the State Department comes back with.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
