turns.text: So two thoughts, Your Honor. First, our consultation claim in this sense is extremely narrow. We don't argue about the levels. We don't argue about the amount. All we say is it has to be about a subject, deliberation about a subject, so they have to talk about country conditions. And you could hold that, Your Honor, and leave aside, just say we're not saying it's okay to police meaningfulness, even though, in other statutes, lower courts do -- you know, consultation claims -- consultation provisions are in other -- other statutes and, you know, the sky doesn't fall. But, if -- if your -- that's Your Honor's concern, just only say it has to be about the topic, and -- and we don't say anything about, you know, meaningfulness in a broader sense. That's my first answer. My second answer is, you know, the State Department actually provided reports because they did care about speaking in one voice for 35 years under this statute. This is in the former senior government officials' brief, a bipartisan brief, including somebody from the first Trump administration talking about the fact that they used to actually look at all the different components of the State Department and talk about this so that they could make sure that the decision was good. There was never a challenge to consultation under that. Even in the first Trump administration --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: You think that sort of elaborate process is necessary --

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: -- under this statute?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No, I do not, Your Honor, I do not. My point is just, you know, it wasn't a problem until the foreign e-mails started. Even in the first Trump administration when there were -- that was the first time there were other TPS challenges. Before that 16 designations -- terminations, never a challenge, right? It started then. Even after that, this -- this consultation claim is only arisen because now they're doing the foreign e-mail.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Justice Barrett sort of was asking a question about -- almost sounded a little bit like harmless error, even if they didn't consult. That's okay because, you know, they were going to make the same decision? How do you deal with that? I mean, this is a due process claim. And we've never said what the final determination is important to due process, correct?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yeah, correct, Your Honor. You know, I think I would say two things about it. The first, there isn't a basis in this record to say that she would have done the same thing if the state, particularly on the armed conflict designation, where national interest is not a criteria, so you have to find --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: That's under the (A) section of the statute?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Correct, that's under (b)(1)(A). There's two designations under Syria. One under armed conflict and the other under extraordinary temporary conditions. Our position is that even under the latter one it is not permissible to consider national interest at the periodic review stage because what is required is that there be review of conditions in the foreign state. And we think when the word "conditions" is used, you know, just a couple lines later, it's referring back to conditions in the foreign state and not criteria, which is what my friend kept saying. And if you look at the -- the word, the name, the label of it is extraordinary and temporary conditions, which is talking about country conditions, (b)(1)(B) also says living conditions. So every time the word "conditions" is used in subsection (b), it's talking about country conditions; national interest is not a condition, right? So that -- that's our -- our argument, our -- our argument on the merits as to the second one. But on the first one, even as to process, there's nothing in this record to tell you that if they had actually consulted, the Secretary would have said I don't care what the State Department says. Maybe she would have said oh, wow, that's not good. And they would have perhaps, you know, led to a different view. And so I think even if harmless error is permissible in this context, there just isn't a basis to find it and it -- it is again important for the government to speak in one voice. And I think that would be the benefit of -- of imposing -- enforcing the consultation requirement here.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Well, I mean, the whole purpose of -- of the TPS is to ensure that the executive is open about what it's doing, correct?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor, transparency is all through the statute, Your Honor.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: And so to the extent that a president says country -- it's not safe for these people to come back or I'm unwilling to say it's safe for those people to come back, Haiti shows that the four groups of people who were sent back, that have gone back, were killed. So I'm not going to say it, but I don't care, I'm still going to end the program, that that's a different impact than saying it's safe --

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: And I --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: -- and I have an alternative reason anyway?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: It absolutely is, Your Honor. And I think it's also important to remember that this issue about whether you can terminate on the basis of national interest, it only arises if the country is still unsafe, the alternative ground, right, it only arises in the country is still unsafe and as to people who have been able to keep their TPS because despite being vetted, 18 months, every 18 months, resubmitting their background, resubmitting criminal history checks, they have been found not to have even a single felony or more than one misdemeanor or any of the other grounds. So we're talking about the power to mass expel people who have done nothing wrong to countries that remain unsafe. And our view is it is unlikely that a refugee protection statute would have given that power to the Secretary.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: What do you do with -- there are two pools here. One is the people who have been given TPS status for a long period of time. And then the new applicants for which there hasn't been checking yet. Could a president come and say the problem -- I'm not going to terminate the program because the country is still not safe but I'm not going to give new applicants permission to stay because I can't vet those guys?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honor. So in the periodic review process, there's three options. You can terminate, you can extend, and if you extend, you can also designate -- designate again. But you don't have to. If you designate again, that updates the date and has the effect of them bringing new people into the eligibility criteria. But the statute doesn't mandate that. It mandates extension if the country is unsafe but it does not mandate designation. That is like a new designation. And so absolutely, the government could take the position either individually or categorically that we're not going to do any new designations, no more TPS holders, but this fixed population, the people who already have it and have come to rely on the fact that if the government is -- determines that their country is unsafe, then they get to stay, they would still -- that closed population would still be protected, Your Honor.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: So that answers the General's position about this being a pull country in some way, that our policy is a pull?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor, and I think my -- my friend for the Miot plaintiffs will also point out that there's no evidence for this -- this claim about the pull factor. I'll leave that to them, but yes, Your Honor --

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: There are --

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: -- there is no need, you can -- you can just solve the problem by saying we're not going to let any new people into the program. We are going to limit our extensions to countries that are unsafe for people who already have TPS.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The people who are here, however, and previously been vetted, no -- there's no new problem with that vetting for them?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: No, Your Honor. In fact, the -- the statute requires that their TPS be rescinded if they commit a felony or become inadmissible, on any of a very broad set of grounds. So it's -- it's extremely narrow protection. But if they -- if they don't, if they do nothing wrong, then -- and their country is still unsafe, the statute requires that they remain protected.

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan?

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Your argument that the national interest claim is reviewable seems harder to me than the procedural argument. And here's why. I mean, I would have thought it's a -- it's just a -- a version of an argument that is made all the time when it comes to administrative action, like you took the wrong factors into account, or, you know, you didn't take the right factors into account. That's a kind of standard part of arbitrary and capricious review. And I would have thought that if this judicial review provision does anything, it basically says don't subject the Secretary's determination to arbitrary and capricious review as we know it. So why should we treat this argument, this national interest argument any differently?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So I think there's some categorical distinction in my head between an argument like oh, you looked at the earthquake recovery in this portion of the country but not in that portion of the country or you didn't consider this evidence about how the armed conflict is in the southern part but not if eastern part. Those are still within the purview of the statutory criteria about armed conflict or temporary living conditions, right? But it's something else if a Secretary says oh, I'm designating the -- I'm terminating the armed conflict designation because there -- there's been earthquake recovery. But earthquake is not a criteria for the armed conflict. It's only a criteria under (b)(1)(B). JUSTICE KAGAN. Well, that makes it sound if there's any legal error attached to the Secretary's determination, review can come in. And is -- is -- is -- are -- are you reading the review provision that way, that it's just about factual errors, not legal errors?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I -- I do think -- I do think there can be -- I mean we're talking about Guerrero-Lasprilla and Wilkinson definition of legal error. Obviously that might be broad. I don't think the Court has to say that those are reviewable. But the claim that we're making here is that the national interest, you heard me say it, right, the national interest is only at the outset, and it's not in the periodic review because periodic review is a conditions analysis whereas national interest is not described as a condition, it's in contradistinction to conditions. That is a pure question of law. You don't need to know anything, anything at all about facts in order to assess that criteria question. And, Your Honor, there --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: But it's also very easy for Congress to write a review provision that's confined to non-legal questions. And that's not what Congress did here.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: That's true, Your Honor, although they also can easily say --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: I mean --

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: -- all questions --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: -- it has nothing to do with like even if I read this statute as saying determination, is with respect to the determination about country conditions, but if -- if you're in that world where the question is like how did you determine country conditions, whether you made a factual error, whether you made a legal error, Congress in this provision seems not to care.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: So I -- I agree that this provision doesn't read fact law into it one way or another. And I -- I think our narrower argument -- Justice Alito had said -- you know, I took the question to be maybe -- maybe I'm not buying your full -- full-bore determination argument, do you have anything to fall back? And what I was saying was, if you -- if you don't want to take the full textual view, then read it against the backdrop of administrative law, where obviously this Court generally or courts generally have the last view on questions of law. But I think if you say no, that's not the -- what they're doing here, so some legal questions are going to be barred, what I would say is whether or not this is within the scope of the determination, that is our -- what we are disputing, right? Because we're saying it's not a country condition because it doesn't use the word "condition" to describe it, and the review provision is limited to conditions in the foreign state. And this is not in the foreign state. So at least that claim, the threshold question of, like, do you get into the reviewability bar or not, that should be reviewable, even if once we're in it, you would say, like, a legal -- a -- a legal dispute about which kinds of conditions should be in it or not, that that would be barred. You know? And we don't -- we don't believe that -- that necessarily is the case either, but just to be clear, like, our claim is -- at the very highest level, it's just about the criteria of even what counts as a condition.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh?

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: How many Syrians have returned to Syria since the end of the Assad regime? And is that of any relevance to what you've been saying about country conditions?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: I mean, I'd say the same thing that I said to you earlier, Your Honor. Two answers. First is it is of no relevance because even if the Secretary is right and the State Department is wrong, it doesn't change the fact that they didn't talk to each other, and the national interest is not a criteria and those are claims that are clearly reviewable under the statute. So, A, that's my answer. Second, it is true that people have -- many people have gone from Lebanon back into Syria, but if we're -- if we're reading the newspaper now and sort of outside the administrative record, there might be good reasons why people are going from southern Lebanon back to Syria if they're having to pick between the two places. And that is not the same thing as saying, oh, we're going from California to Syria. And so I don't think the fact that you have this mass movement of people is necessarily indicative of whether it is safe to go there or not. As I said, there is still active armed conflict. There's bombing happening now in Syria. So, you know, it may be better or worse. Some people say the mortality rate is higher. I haven't -- you know, I don't know. But, anyway, yeah, that -- I think -- I think it does not answer the question ultimately, even though -- even if it did, we still should win.

turns.name: BRETT KAVANAUGH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson?

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So I'm interested in the standards applicable to our decision-making in this case. And one of them is the thought that even if "determination" could be read to mean different things, the final conclusion or close to it, versus the final conclusion plus the antecedent steps, I thought we had a presumption of reviewability that was supposed to apply to our interpretive analysis in a situation like this. So am I wrong about that?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honor. It's applied in Bowen, in McNary, in Catholic Social Services, and, of course, in Guerrero-Lasprilla, you know, and -- and Wilkinson.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So when Justice Thomas says, well, the background is that we wouldn't interpret this if we're sort of trying to figure out what "determination" is, we -- we -- we wouldn't allow for you to review it, I think the opposite is true. In other words, there's some confusion about the express -- the scope of the express determination -- the express review bar. I thought our rules under our precedents say you're supposed to interpret it narrowly.

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, Your Honor. Two things on this. First, the presumption is clear that they have to show clear and convincing evidence. So the question is, you know, is what we have said by hooking it to "determine" or read it against the hundred years of administrative law good enough to just get above what would be needed, you know, to beat clear and convincing. And I think it is. And the second thing I'd say on that subject is, Your Honor, Biden v. Texas, from just a couple of years ago, this Court holds the APA governs the DHS's parole policy, and it has to be reasonable and reasonably explained against -- and it reaches that holding, every justice of this Court endorses that idea in the face of a jurisdiction-stripping argument which the government makes about the scope of the injunction. You know, all of that I'm sure you all remember. And so it's both true that, as a general matter, this Court has applied the presumption in both large and small immigration cases, and also that it has done it particularly in a context like this one where the issue is about whether Mexico, you know, basically the -- had to be -- the U.S. had to be forced to negotiate with Mexico. And so --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: All right. And my second -- my second issue about standards, is there a clear error standard that is applicable to the district court's findings here, findings of fact, for example, about whether or not there was likely discriminatory intent with respect to this policy?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honor. It is both true -- it's double deference, I would argue, because it's both here on preliminary relief, there may be more evidence to come if the case is allowed to survive, certainly the constitutional claim is going to be allowed to survive, given the -- on -- on jurisdiction anyway, and, in addition, because factual findings are reviewed for clear error in general, then it is true that the clear error operates there. I think that now, since we have the e-mail about consultation and we all agree that that's the scope of it, it's not really relevant. You can read that one page of our brief --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Or it's just so obviously not an error, not a clear error as a result of that evidence, right?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Well, yes, Your Honor, absolutely. I mean --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: I mean, we're still applying the clear error -- you're not saying jettison the clear error or standard; you're saying look at this evidence. If the district court found it to be that -- the e-mail in terms of consultation or the discriminatory intent in terms of what the President said, our -- our burden is to determine whether or not she made a clear error in her fact finding related to those issues, correct?

turns.name: AHILAN T. ARULANANTHAM
turns.text: Yes, absolutely, Your Honor. And the last thing I would just say about that is, on the pretext claim, where I know there -- maybe everybody doesn't think that we have all the evidence, it's not the evidence that was in Commerce because it was a full trial in Commerce. I think in that context too it is relevant we are here on preliminary relief because the district court was looking at it and that's -- that's what you've got.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Pipoly.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court: For decades, administrations of both parties successfully terminated TPS designations without inviting litigation. They did so by following the process Congress set forth in the TPS statute. The termination of Haiti's TPS was different. It was not the result of the mandatory review process but was instead a preordained result driven by the President's resolve to end TPS for Haiti, no matter what. The reasons Secretary Noem gave for the termination were pretextual. The DHS documents that we already lodged with this Court show that the Secretary's purported review was a sham. Agency staff was "forced" to include rationales for termination that had no empirical support. The true reason for the termination of the -- for the termination is the President's racial animus towards non-white immigrants and bare dislike of Haitians, in particular. The President has disparaged Haitian TPS holders specifically as undesirables from a "shithole country," and days after falsely accusing them of "eating the dogs and eating the cats of Americans," he vowed that he would terminate Haiti's TPS. And that is exactly what happened. Recognizing all this, the district court correctly postponed the termination. This Court should affirm. And I welcome the Court's questions.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: What weight do you -- how would you interpret the jurisdiction-stripping provision?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: No different than the Doe plaintiffs do, Justice Thomas.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: More generally, is there anything that your friend said that you disagree with?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: No, Justice -- Chief Justice -- Mr. Chief Justice. My apologies.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Whatever.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Can I ask about your equal protection claim?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Certainly.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Is this -- is this a -- a race claim or is it a national origin claim, or does it matter?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: It's -- it's -- it's a -- it's certainly a race-based claim, we would argue, given the -- as -- as some of the questioning earlier got to, the evidence certainly suggests racial animus, which, under -- which the Arlington Heights framework is specifically designed to suss out. The -- the statements, "I would like fewer people from places like Haiti," that were described with the word that I won't repeat again, and countries like Norway and Denmark and Sweden, as Justice Sotomayor suggested earlier, that's very close to what we had in Arlington Heights itself. So we do frame this as a race-based claim. We do think it's racially motivated, particularly in light of the cross-cutting terminations we've seen. As the district court in our case put it, 13 up, 13 down, all non-white. While --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: So is -- is that it? It's -- it's not Haiti particularly; it's all these countries have people of color as opposed to Denmark and Scandinavian -- you know, Scandinavia generally and whatever?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Sure. I certainly think that the record supports the idea that the President in particular has focused in on Haitians, but it is broader than that. Haitians are our plaintiffs. But the relevant compare -- the relevant group here is -- is all TPS countries, all of which are non-white.

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: And -- and what if one thinks that -- you know, if -- you said there was a determination that no matter what, there was going to be a change to Haiti's TPS status. You know, there seems to have been a pretty clear determination that all TPS status should go, right? There are no -- there's -- there's -- there's no TPS status that hasn't been renounced. So how does that fact -- factor into this equal protection claim?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Sure. Our position is is that you cannot have, for whatever reason, race-based or otherwise, a pre -- a -- an agenda to end TPS because these are country-specific --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: Quite -- quite right. But that's a different kind of claim. I -- I guess I'm just wondering like how to think about the racial component of this, if there seems to have been, you know, wherever and whatever TPS I can find, it's not going to exist tomorrow.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I'm sorry, I'm not following. Well, the race-based, you know --

turns.name: ELENA KAGAN
turns.text: You -- you know, that there's -- you -- you can -- you can argue that there was just like an across the board, we have to get rid of all these TPS and the statutory requirements weren't followed and -- and -- and all of that, but -- but the objection of this racial component into it, I guess I don't quite see how that operates when all of these programs went.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, again, I would point you back to both the President's statements and the Secretary's statements. The Secretary herself described people from Haiti and from 18 other all non-white countries as killers, leaches, entitlement junkies saying we don't want them, not one, while simultaneously enacting a policy, another humanitarian form of relief, for white and only white South Africans. So if you want the comparator group, that's part of it. And -- and it's true that the program, the refugee program under which the South -- the white South Africans were admitted is not TPS as such, but both statutes are -- are motivated by the same policy from Congress -- motivated by the same policy. They're both humanitarian programs. In both TPS and with the special refugee program, it's the United States saying these folks are facing some hardship in their home country, at least that's the stated basis, and we're going to let them in. So it's -- it's not -- it's -- it's the President's statements in which there is a comparative group, white versus -- non-white countries versus white countries, and it's the fact that you've got the -- the -- that -- those sort of sentiments being art -- articulated into policy

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: But more directly --

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: -- with regard to South African --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: -- more directly to Justice Kagan's point, is it -- is it your view that the reason why the President was saying all of the TPS programs have to go is because the TPS program relates to countries that have large minority or large racial compositions?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Yes, that's exactly right, Justice.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: In other words, the motivation for getting rid of all of them is that these programs "benefit" these kinds of people.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That -- that -- yes, that's exactly right. And I apologize if I didn't follow that but, yes, that is -- that is absolutely correct. And under Arlington Heights, the -- the racial motivation need be only one of many factors. In every government policy I can imagine, there is a facially-legitimate reason given for the termination and the -- for the government action. The Arlington Heights framework exists precisely for the purpose of sussing out whether impermissible racial considerations were part of -- were -- were impermissibly in the mix.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: But isn't it the case that TPS was terminated for quite a list of countries. And I -- I -- I -- I can't seem to find the particular page of the transcript where the district court goes through them all. And, yes, none of those is a Nordic country. But -- and I don't like dividing up the people of the world arbitrarily into three racial groups, but you -- you say they're all non-white. And that's the -- that's the distinguishing characteristic?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That is the distinguishing characteristic that the district court held. But I would -- I would emphasize, Justice Alito, that --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: But do you think that if -- if you put Syrians, Turks, Greeks, and other people who live around the Mediterranean in a lineup, do you think you could say those people are -- are -- that all of them, are they all non-white?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I understand that Syrians I think may be classified as white for purposes of the State Department. I -- or -- or for under -- under certain government -- you know, certain government programs but again, I think race is -- I think, you know, you'd have to pole the public to know what they think the race of a Syrian is. I certainly think they're not white --

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Pole -- pole the American people? Do they -- do they think Syrians are white?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I -- I'm -- I wouldn't think that most would, Justice Alito.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: Really?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I really don't.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: How about Turks?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I honestly haven't considered what racial component I would sort Turks into.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: How about Greek's?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I -- I don't know the answer to that either.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: How about southern Italians?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, certainly -- certainly 120 years ago when we had our last wave of European immigration, southern Italians were not considered white. So I think our concept of these things evolves over time.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: How about Spaniards?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I think same answer about 120 years ago, I don't think they were considered white.

turns.name: SAMUEL ALITO
turns.text: You have a really large -- you have a really broad definition of who's white and who's not white. As I said, I don't like dividing the people of the world into these groups.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I -- I understand. I -- I would that say even under this Court's rationality jurisprudence if you look at cases like Moreno, it is not necessary for us to get strict scrutiny to win here because irrespective of how you do the classification at issue here, under those Court's -- under those decisions -- excuse me, under those precedents, bare dislike of -- of an unpopular group is a sufficient basis to find that rational basis is not even satisfied.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Given your understanding of the review bar, wouldn't your APA arguments be exactly the same if there were no review bar? In other words, what function does it -- with respect to your APA arguments, in what way does the review bar restrict what you -- what -- what you want to argue?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I -- I would give the same answer that counsel for the Doe plaintiffs gave, which is that there are -- that determination has the same meaning in the TPS statute that it had in the SAW statute at issue in the McNary case, that in that case, the antecedent obligations procedurally were subject to judicial review even if the substantive determination was not.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: On that score, counsel, you agreed that the determination -- the country conditions no longer meet the criteria is unreviewable?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Yes, the Secretary's substantive --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: And final determination under what is it (B), right, (4)(B) -- (3)(B), sorry? That's unreviewable?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: The Secretary's substantive conclusion as to the existence or non-existence --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well, it's a determination, right, and that's what the statute says.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Correct. And that's how we define determination.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Yeah. And -- and that takes effect once it's published in the Federal Register plus 60 days or something like that, under -- under (3)(B), right?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That's correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Okay. And that's the determination and that's the effect of the statute, but you say that a court can enjoin it anyway.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: No, they can -- well, for -- we didn't get an injunction here. We got 705 relief --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: 705 postponement. Yeah, I mean, I'm -- I'm just looking at what the court said. I think in the Syria case, said that the -- the defendants' termination of TPS status for Syrians is hereby postponed. And the D.C. Circuit in your case said the district court's postponed termination, right?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That's correct. That's Section 705 of the --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: How is that not judicial review of the Secretary's determination?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, I would say that, again, the -- the claim --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I understand your process point, that you want to look at some antecedent things. But how can it not be judicial review of the determination if you're postponing the determination?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Because determination -- well, it -- I -- I can't -- it's difficult for me to answer that question without pointing out

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: It's difficult for me to answer the question too.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, no, probably for different reasons.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Well, no, I don't know. I'm asking -- I'm -- I'm just-- I'm struggling with that.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: No, I understand. The question comes down to do you define determination as coextensive with a broader term like decision. And we see --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: No, no, no. I'm -- I'm working within your framework for purposes of this question. You know, (3)(B) says once the attorney general, but we all agree that's the Secretary, makes the determination, the country conditions are no longer met, the determination decision takes effect, published in the Federal Register, plus 60 days, something like that. And we -- we all agree on that. And that -- that's what the statute says about the effectiveness of the determination.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Right. We have -- we -- the -- the final agency action here that was -- that was postponed is as counsel --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Is the determination.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: It is the termination, not the determination, which is not subject to judicial review.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: That -- that's what you got?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That is consistent with McNary. It's consistent with Bowen.

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: Counsel, is your point that the -- that judicial review runs to the claim? In other words, what -- what is happening in the judicial review bar, when it says there's no judicial review, it means that the court cannot consider the claim that's being made but that's different than what the court having considered the claim ultimately does?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Yeah. That's exactly right. I mean, again --

turns.name: KETANJI BROWN JACKSON
turns.text: So at the end of the day, if the court considers a claim about a defect in the procedure, and thinks it likely and, therefore, postpones the termination while that claim is under review, that's not the same thing as reviewing the ultimate determination?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That's exactly right. The determination here has the same meaning that it had in McNary and Bowen, which is the substantive existence -- the existence substantively of the -- of the -- of the conditions for designation; i.e., is Haiti still safe? The final agency action at issue here is the termination that was published in the Federal Register.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: I -- I appreciate all of Justice Jackson's points and yours, but the statute says that determination is effective basically automatically, right? And it -- it tells us when it's effective. And it tells us how it's effective. And that's what the statute -- that's what Congress told us, is once that determination is made, boom, it goes. And -- and I -- I'm just struggling with how -- how that -- that could be true and -- and yet it could also be true that -- that judicial review postponing that -- that termination decision is not judicial review of that judicial determination -- of that determination.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Right. Because the termination decision, the final agency action, includes substantially more than the determination. It includes things like when the --

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: It includes antecedent things, of course --

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Correct.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: -- that feed into that determination. I -- I appreciate that. Okay. All right.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Right.

turns.name: NEIL GORSUCH
turns.text: Thank you.

turns.name: AMY CONEY BARRETT
turns.text: Would you like to address -- would you like to address the General's point, the Solicitor General's point, that this would drive a truck through the judicial review bar?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: I don't think it would and no more so than, again, McNary or Bowen already did. And -- and I would remind the Court that in Bowen and McNary -- excuse me, in McNary, the plaintiffs in that case won, and maybe this is responsive to Justice Gorsuch's point. Even though they were challenging the procedure by which their SAW determinations was made, they still obtained injunctions and invalidation of the underlying determinations that they were challenging. So this tension that we're identifying between the process and the outcome is one that this Court has been -- and that the law has been comfortable with for over 30 years now. As far as it driving a hole through the review bar, I would come back to the exact same point -- well, to a similar point, which is the determination is -- is -- is off the table. We agree with that. Congress could not have intended, we say, for the -- for things -- for these antecedent considerations not to be considered because, when it enacted the TPS statute, it already had the benefit of Bowen, and after it passed the review bar, Congress -- several years after it passed the review bar, Congress enacted IIRIRA, in which it -- it retained the language from Bowen -- from Bowen, from McNary. So it's reasonable to read the review bar in this case as consistent with that in Bowen and McNary. In other words, Congress knows how to write broader language encompassing more than a specific determination. It could write all questions of law are fact. And, in fact, in some other sections of Title VIII, it even writes language that we think would preclude procedure and process claims, like in -- in another section of Title VIII, it refers to all procedures and policies. That's 1252(a)(2)(A)(iv). So Congress knows how to write broader language if it wants to, but it chose not to do so here, even within the background of Bowen and McNary.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Thomas, anything further?

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: How exactly does your equal protection argument work? The Equal Protection Clause applies to states.

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, this is a claim that arises under the Fifth Amendment -- the Fifth Amendment's equal protection guarantee.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: Of life, liberty, and property?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That is the equal protection component of the Fifth Amendment due process guarantee. That's correct.

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: So how does it work?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Well, this Court has held repeatedly --

turns.name: CLARENCE THOMAS
turns.text: No. How does your claim work? How do you get to the Fifth Amendment?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: Because the Fifth Amendment constrains the federal government in the same way that the Fourteenth Amendment constrains states.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Alito, anything further? Justice Sotomayor?

turns.name: SONIA SOTOMAYOR
turns.text: The Fifth Amendment says the federal government can't discriminate on the basis of race, correct?

turns.name: GEOFFREY M. PIPOLY
turns.text: That's exactly right. And -- and the other thing I would -- I would emphasize that I was trying to get at earlier is that even under this case -- this Court's rationality cases, we still win. Remember the -- the facts of Moreno. There was a facially plausible FDA program that did not allow unmarried households to receive food stamps. This Court nonetheless said that there was something else at play there, animus against a particular group, a bare dislike of a particular group. And the President's statements, regardless of whether you consider them inherently racial or some other type of classification, reflect a bare dislike for Haitians in particular.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Justice Kagan, anything further? Justice Gorsuch? Justice Kavanaugh? Justice Barrett? Justice Jackson? Thank you, counsel. Rebuttal, General?

turns.name: D. JOHN SAUER
turns.text: Very briefly, Mr. Chief Justice. Congress balanced the risk that -- by enacting a judicial review bar, Congress balanced the risk that there might be some decision that's erroneous or baseless or off-base against -- that would evade judicial review against the risk of what we're living through here, which is judicial micromanagement of the sorts of foreign-policy-laden determinations and decisions that are naturally conferred upon the -- the political branches. Justice Alito, turning to your "convoy of trucks" question, if you look at the briefing in this case, I think it vividly illustrates the -- the concern that any exception that they put forth, and the exception morphs when they talk about it with different -- you know, different -- different formulations, any one of those exceptions creates a -- a -- an exception that would eviscerate the statutory -- or the judicial review bar here. So, if you look, for example, at the Syria Respondents, the claims they raise, they raise the consultation claim, but as I pointed out earlier, even those consultation claims are starting to bake in substantive criteria. In other words, the district courts are saying, well, you did consult, but your consultation wasn't thorough enough. Therefore, we give you a D-plus. Come back when you've got a B-minus consultation. Maybe we'll let you terminate at that time. And it gets even more striking when you get to their claims and things about the national interest criteria, which is unquestionably a substantive criteria. And then even further, if you look, for example, at the Syria Respondents, their pretext claim, they say, well, we're raising a pretext claim and here's four reasons why we think this decision was pretextual. Reason 3 is a long discussion of how they think the Secretary got the administrative record wrong and made the wrong kinds of judgments and so forth. It gets even more striking when you read the Haiti Respondents' brief, where, in the 11 pages or so in which they discuss the -- the merits of their claims, by the second or third page, they've kind of abandoned any pretense that what they're raising is procedural, and they're raising the whole panoply of substantive challenge -- APA-type challenges to this particular decision. So, to the extent there is a -- you know, a -- a -- a -- a judicial -- or any exception to the judicial review bar here, their own briefs, I think, demonstrate that it's going to collapse under its own weight. There's been reference to the presidential directives that we're supposed to provide. There is a presidential directive that was provided. It was provided in the executive order. And the President directed the Secretary to ensure that TPS designations are "appropriately limited in scope" and only as long as necessary to achieve the -- the textual directives in the statute. And that is what the -- that is what the Secretary did here. And then, Justice Gorsuch, as to your question, I do think it's helpful to end this case by look -- or end this argument by looking at their prayer for relief in their complaints, which says we are challenging the termination decision as to these two -- these two countries. We are saying that that termination decision was unlawful. It should be declared unlawful. It should be set aside under the APA. It should be postponed under Section 705. And I think, at that point, at a very high level, we are looking at a -- a request for judicial review of the termination determination, and that is exactly what the statute bars. Thank you.

turns.name: JOHN ROBERTS
turns.text: Thank you, counsel. The case is submitted.
